strengths: The core idea—replacing pixel-history conditioning with a persistent, dynamically evolving latent 3D world-frame (environment + camera + learned deferred renderer)—is well-motivated and a genuine paradigm shift for interactive world models, directly addressing the spatial-memory bottleneck of AR video diffusion models.

The system is technically substantive: a 3D rectified-flow DiT for world-frame dynamics with absolute XYZ positional embeddings, a residual-parameterized camera transformer, and a pixel denoiser conditioned on a depth-ordered screen-space projection (Algorithm 1, Fig. 4), with components trained separately and composed at inference via a simple noise-augmentation trick without fine-tuning.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: a 28-participant, 800+ rollout user study with per-metric rubrics, head-to-head score-delta matrices (Figs. 9–12), per-condition breakdowns (Tables 9–12), and complementary FVD, with clear protocol details (warm-start conditions, calibration trials) in Appendix B.

Results show large, consistent gains over Oasis and WorldMem (FVD 116–209 vs. 596–706; user scores ~2.6–3.0 vs. ~1.5–1.9), and the paper demonstrates genuinely new capabilities: single-image 3D outpainting/initialization (Fig. 13), mid-episode 3D world edits (Fig. 6), and off-screen dynamics (Fig. 7).

The limitations discussion is candid and specific (ground-truth 3D supervision requirement, exposure-bias drift over 2000-step episodes in Fig. 14, finite agent-centered spatial extent), and these are not hidden from the abstract or conclusion.
Reproducibility is reasonable: detailed hyperparameter tables (Tables 2–8), inference pseudocode, dataset construction (460h of Luanti/Craftium gameplay), and compute budgets are provided.
weaknesses: The method depends on ground-truth 3D voxel supervision from the game engine, plus ground-truth camera states; this restricts applicability to simulators with privileged 3D access and is a major scope limitation, acknowledged but not yet resolved (no experiment even with a weak proxy such as predicted/synthetic 3D annotations).

Baseline comparisons have a domain-mismatch confound: PERSIST is trained on ~40M interactions from Luanti/Craftium, while Oasis and WorldMem are evaluated on their native Minecraft/MineDojo data. The authors avoid training-domain shift but this makes the cross-method comparison in Table 1 imperfect for isolating the representation from the data/setup.

Evaluation is confined to a single voxel-based domain (Luanti/MineDojo); the fixed 48^3 agent-centered world-frame raises open questions about scaling to large, realistic, non-voxel environments, which are not empirically probed.

Some architectural design choices are asserted rather than ablated, e.g., channel-allocation biasing of w2D vs. ō, the 10% noise augmentation, the depth-peeling layer count l, and the residual camera parameterization; the Oasis-as-ablation framing covers only the w2D-guidance component.

PERSIST-XL does not consistently improve over PERSIST-S in human ratings (and slightly loses on 3D consistency, +0.21 for S), so the relationship between 3D representation capacity and quality is not fully characterized.

Long-horizon stability is improved but not solved: Fig. 14 documents recurring glitches (disappearing geometry, texture drift, collision errors) from exposure bias, and PERSIST's memory is still bounded by the 48^3 region, so the headline 'persistent memory' claim holds only locally.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: replacing pixel-history conditioning and key-frame retrieval with an actively maintained latent 3D world-frame addresses a genuine, recognized weakness of AR interactive world models (finite context windows, viewpoint-dependent memory).

The evaluation is more thorough than typical for this area: a large user study (800+ evaluations, 28 participants) with a defined protocol, complementary FVD measurements, head-to-head score matrices, and per-evaluation-set breakdowns in the appendix. Both quantitative and human evaluations consistently favor PERSIST over Oasis and WorldMem (e.g., FVD 116-209 vs. 596-706; user ratings ~2.5-3.0 vs. ~1.5-1.9).

The demonstration of emergent and design-enabled capabilities is convincing and goes beyond quality metrics: mid-episode 3D world edits, explicit 3D initialization improving results (PERSIST-XL+w0), and off-screen dynamics (e.g., a cave filling with water) that manifest later on-screen.

The methodology section is reproducible in spirit: architectures, hyperparameters, training compute, inference logic (full pseudocode in Algorithms 1-2), user study interface and instructions, and FVD computation are all documented in the appendix.

The limitations discussion is honest and specific rather than perfunctory: reliance on ground-truth 3D supervision, exposure bias with concrete failure examples over a 2000-step episode (Figure 14), and the finite local memory region, each with a concrete research direction.
weaknesses: The central requirement of ground-truth 3D supervision (48^3 voxel grids and camera extrinsics from the simulator) severely limits applicability. This is fine for Minecraft-like voxel engines where 3D state is trivially extractable, but it is unclear how the approach extends to real video, in-the-wild footage, or even non-voxel simulators. The authors acknowledge this but it substantially narrows the contribution's reach and makes the setting arguably the easiest possible one for the proposed representation.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled. Oasis and WorldMem use publicly available checkpoints trained on their own Minecraft data, evaluated in MineDojo, while PERSIST is trained on ~460 hours of Craftium data. Although the authors avoid domain shift by evaluating baselines on MineDojo, the methods are not trained on the same data distribution, so the claimed superiority may partly reflect training data or inference configuration differences rather than the representation itself. WorldMem is also given 600 ground-truth warm-start frames yet still underperforms, which is surprising and warrants closer analysis.

The headline configuration (PERSIST-XL+w0) conditions on a ground-truth world-frame at initialization, which inflates its numbers relative to the more practically relevant setting (single image initialization). The gap between PERSIST-XL and PERSIST-XL+w0 in Table 1 (e.g., FVD 181 vs. 116) suggests initialization quality is a major confound not fully disentangled.

Inference-time practicality is not addressed: the pipeline runs three denoisers (world, camera, pixel) with 20 denoising steps per frame plus 3D-VAE decode and depth-peeled rasterization per timestep. There is no report of generation speed, so claims of suitability for interactive experiences cannot be verified; comparing against real-time systems like Oasis on this axis matters.

Evaluation is confined to a single voxel-based environment family, with scripted policies (forward/backward/orbit/free play). There is no evidence on action-conditioned object interactions (block breaking/placement), agent-level dynamics, or generalization to unseen interaction types, which are the actual hard cases for world models.

Some evidence is anecdotal: the off-screen dynamics and world-editing capabilities are demonstrated with single examples (Figures 6-7) rather than systematically quantified; emergence claims would benefit from controlled probes.

User study results lack statistical significance testing; margins between PERSIST-S and PERSIST-XL are small and the authors themselves describe several differences as 'too narrow to call', yet Table 1 bolds PERSIST-S on some metrics without inferential support.

The system's complexity is high (five separately trained models combined with noise augmentation and no end-to-end finetuning), and the reported glitches (terrain clipping, texture drift, blocks appearing/disappearing) indicate the approach does not yet solve autoregressive drift, only mitigates it.

strengths: The core idea — replacing pixel-history conditioning with an actively generated, evolving latent 3D world-frame queried via a camera model and a differentiable projection/rasterization operator — is a genuinely novel and well-motivated paradigm for interactive world models, clearly framed against the known failure modes of rolling-window and key-frame retrieval approaches.

The methodology is technically solid: the decomposition into world-frame prediction, camera prediction, and world-to-pixel generation is clearly specified, with concrete treatment of important practical issues such as exposure bias (diffusion forcing plus noise augmentation to allow component-wise training without fine-tuning), residual camera re-parameterization, and depth-peeling rasterization for pixel-level alignment.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: a large user study (800+ rollout evaluations, 28 participants, head-to-head paired comparisons with detailed protocol in Appendix B), FVD computed on held-out worlds, per-set breakdowns, and head-to-head score-delta matrices in the appendix. Gains over Oasis and WorldMem are consistent and substantial across all metrics and evaluation modes.

The paper demonstrates novel capabilities enabled by the explicit 3D state (single-image 3D scene initialization with outpainting diversity, mid-episode 3D editing, off-screen dynamics persisting unobserved), which go beyond incremental metric improvements and illustrate the practical value of the representation.

Reproducibility support is strong: full architecture/hyperparameter tables for all components, training cost breakdowns, inference logic given as pseudocode (including the w0-conditioned variant), dataset construction details, and an honest, detailed limitations section (ground-truth 3D supervision requirement, exposure-bias drift documented over a 2000-step rollout in Figure 14, finite spatial memory) with a concrete future-work roadmap.

The comparison setup is reasonably careful about domain shift: baselines trained on Minecraft are evaluated on MineDojo data rather than the authors' Craftium domain, and the Oasis comparison is additionally framed as an ablation of PERSIST without 3D guidance.
weaknesses: The approach relies on ground-truth 3D voxel annotations and camera states from the simulator during training, which substantially restricts applicability to environments where such supervision is extractable; the limitation is acknowledged honestly, but it does cap the significance of the contribution relative to pixel-only methods, and no experiment (e.g., noisy or partially synthetic 3D supervision) probes how robust the method is to relaxed supervision.

Baseline comparability is imperfect: PERSIST is trained on ~460 hours of Craftium data in the evaluation domain, while Oasis and WorldMem are pre-trained on Minecraft data and evaluated zero-shot in MineDojo; even with matched inference configurations, some of the large gaps (e.g., FVD 181 vs 596) may partly reflect domain fit rather than the memory mechanism alone. A same-domain retrain or fine-tune of at least one baseline would strengthen the claim.

Ablations of key design choices are missing or thin: the channel-budget bias favoring w2D over o, the Plücker embeddings, the 10% noise augmentation rate, and the choice of context window sizes are asserted but not systematically studied; the S-vs-XL analysis is included, which helps, but the dependence of results on these hyperparameters is unclear.

User-study absolute scores are modest (best overall score 3.0/5, and ground truth still strongly preferred in every head-to-head comparison), so the method improves relative standing but does not yet reach practical long-horizon fidelity; the quantitative definition of 'significantly outperforms' (e.g., statistical tests on user ratings) is not reported.

Inference cost and latency of the full three-model pipeline (world denoiser + camera model + pixel denoiser, 20 denoising steps per frame plus rasterization) are not characterized, leaving open whether the framework is viable for the real-time interactive use cases motivating the work; the closed-source frontier comparison (Genie 3) is acknowledged but not addressable.

Minor presentation issues: inconsistent naming between 'PERSIST-S' in Table 1 and 'PERSIST-Base' in the appendix matrices (Figure 9–12), the 'free play' vs 'circle around' evaluation-mode naming, and the L value (number of depth layers) of the projection operator is not specified in the main text, which slightly hampers reproduction of the projection machinery.

strengths: The core idea—replacing pixel-history/keyframe-retrieval conditioning with an actively generated, persistent latent 3D world-frame queried via a learned camera model—is a well-motivated and genuinely novel paradigm for interactive world models, cleanly bridging learned AR video diffusion with classical simulator/game-engine design.

The technical formulation is carefully worked out: rectified-flow denoisers for world-frame, camera, and pixel prediction; a differentiable depth-peeled rasterization-based projection operator; diffusion-forcing-style training plus noise augmentation to allow component-wise training without fine-tuning; and support for generating the initial world-frame from a single RGB image, which removes the need for 3D conditioning at inference.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: FVD and per-timestep FID over 600-frame rollouts against retrained, identically-formulated baselines (Oasis, WorldMem); informative ablations (PERSIST-S, No-3D-Upscale, Camera-GT, PERSIST+w0); an 800+ video human study with 28 participants, head-to-head score matrices, and per-policy breakdowns; and inference-speed benchmarks including a 3x speed configuration.

Demonstrated emergent capabilities (mid-episode 3D edits, off-screen dynamics driving on-screen effects, self-correction over 2000-step rollouts) go beyond the headline metrics and substantiate the claim that the 3D state is a persistent, causally meaningful representation rather than a rendering cache.

Limitations are treated honestly and constructively: reliance on ground-truth 3D supervision, finite spatial memory, exposure-bias drift artifacts (documented step-by-step in Figure 13), and non-real-time inference are all explicitly acknowledged, with a concrete roadmap (2D-to-3D annotation, rollout post-training, 3D memory banks). Appendices provide substantial implementation detail (architectures, hyperparameters, algorithms), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on privileged ground-truth 3D supervision (48^3 voxel grids with semantic labels and camera states from the simulator) significantly restricts applicability to simulators or 3D-annotated data; this is acknowledged but means the central claims are demonstrated in essentially one domain (Luanti/Craftium voxel worlds), and generalization to photorealistic, non-voxel environments remains unproven.

The human study compares PERSIST (trained on Craftium) against released Oasis/WorldMem checkpoints evaluated in a different domain (Minedojo); although the authors attempt to control for domain bias (reporting <0.15 score difference on ground-truth videos across domains), this confound weakens the human-evaluation comparison relative to the carefully controlled quantitative comparison.

FVD/FID are known to be imperfect proxies for the properties the paper most cares about (3D consistency, physical plausibility); the authors themselves note that Camera-GT introduces physical inconsistencies (agent phasing through terrain) invisible to FVD, yet no quantitative metric for camera/world consistency (e.g., collision accuracy or geometric error in the 3D state) is provided to substantiate those qualitative observations.

The world-frame is a fixed 48^3 cuboid centred on the agent, so spatial memory is actually quite limited despite the framing of 'persistent spatial memory'; long-range revisits beyond this region are not addressed, and the paper does not quantify memory scale limitations empirically.

Component-wise training with only noise augmentation to bridge train/inference distribution gaps leaves residual exposure-bias artifacts (Figure 13) and the pipeline is not trained or fine-tuned end-to-end; it would be useful to see evidence on how sensitive system stability is to this design choice.

Minor presentation issues: duplicated WorldMem citations (2025a/2025b), truncated/garbled arXiv identifiers in several references, and some figures (e.g., Figure 5) would benefit from clearer indication of what the eval actions/policies were per column.

strengths: The core idea — replacing pixel-history conditioning with an actively generated, persistent latent 3D world-frame queried by a camera model — is well motivated and cleanly framed as a 'proxy hidden state' (Section 4), with a sensible decomposition into world-frame prediction, camera prediction, and world-to-pixel rendering.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: FVD and per-timestep FID over 600-frame episodes (Tables 1, Figure 6), a well-designed human study with 28 participants and 800+ rollouts including head-to-head score matrices (Appendix C), and informative ablations (PERSIST-S, No-3D-Upscale, Camera-GT) that isolate which component drives the gains (e.g., the finding that the 3D representation is robust to 512× spatial compression).

Novel capabilities are demonstrated convincingly: single-image 3D initialisation with diverse outpainting (Figure 12), mid-episode 3D edits (Figure 7), and emergent off-screen dynamics such as a cave filling with water while unobserved (Figure 8).

Limitations are handled honestly and constructively: ground-truth 3D supervision, finite spatial memory, exposure bias (Figure 13 gives a candid artifact timeline), and non-real-time inference are all discussed with concrete future-work directions.
The paper is generally well written, with clear formalism (Section 3), complete architecture and hyperparameter tables, and inference algorithms in the appendix that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Scope and generality are restricted by the central design assumption: the world-frame is trained with ground-truth voxel labels from a voxel engine (Luanti) where the 3D state is trivially extractable. The paper is therefore somewhat circular — it shows that a model given (a learned version of) the simulator's state representation beats models that only see pixels. Generality to non-voxel, non-annotated domains is untested and deferred to future work.

Baseline fairness in the human study is questionable: Oasis and WorldMem were evaluated using author-released models trained on Minecraft data, in a different domain (Minedojo), while PERSIST models were presumably tuned for the Luanti/Craftium domain. The authors' mitigation (no domain preference for ground-truth videos) is helpful but does not fully eliminate the concern that domain mismatch depresses baseline ratings; WorldMem is also given 400 ground-truth frames to seed its memory bank, a very different operating regime.

Several quantitative gaps are left unexplained or unaddressed: WorldMem's FVD is missing at 400/600 frames in Table 1 without justification; FVD differences between PERSIST variants rely on a single 168-rollout evaluation set with no variance or significance reporting; and FVD/FID are known to be unreliable for long-horizon, content-diverse generations, so quantitative conclusions lean heavily on the (imperfectly controlled) human study.

The learned camera model introduces physical inconsistencies (agent phasing through terrain, Figure 11), yet FVD is essentially unchanged versus Camera-GT, underscoring that the automated metrics do not capture the properties the paper claims matter most (e.g., physical plausibility of the camera trajectory).

The system is very heavy (dozens of GPU-days across four separately trained components, ~30GB-scale models) and does not achieve real-time inference (1.13 FPS at best), limiting practical interactive use despite the paper's framing around user experience; the '3× speed-up' variant still degrades FVD noticeably.

Scalability of the world-frame representation is bounded by construction: memory is a fixed 48^3 voxel cuboid centred on the agent, so the claimed 'persistence' is local; very long-horizon coherence beyond this region remains unaddressed except as future work.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: replacing pixel-history conditioning with an actively generated, persistent latent 3D state (world-frame + camera + renderer) directly addresses the finite-context-window limitation of AR world models, and the design is well grounded in the graphics/simulation analogy (Section 4, Figure 1).

Substantial empirical evidence: FVD evaluated at 200/400/600-frame horizons (Table 1) shows PERSIST maintains near-flat quality (129→148) while pixel-history baselines degrade sharply (Oasis 409→875); per-timestep FID (Figure 6) corroborates stability over 600 steps and even 2000-step episodes (Figure 13).

Well-designed ablations that isolate the contribution of each component (3D-S vs 3D-XL token budget, No-3D-Upscale, Camera-GT), including the interesting finding that the 3D representation tolerates up to 512× spatial compression while rendering quality depends on the upscaled latent (Section 6.1).

A complementary human study with 28 participants and 800+ paired evaluations (Table 2, Appendices B–C), which appropriately addresses known biases of FVD/FID and includes head-to-head delta matrices; the finding that PERSIST-S matches PERSIST perceptually despite worse FVD is an honest and useful nuance.

New capabilities enabled by the representation are convincingly demonstrated: single-image 3D initialization with diversity (Figure 12), mid-episode 3D world edits (Figure 7), and off-screen dynamics causing emergent on-screen effects (Figure 8).

Honest and thorough limitations discussion (Appendix E): reliance on ground-truth 3D supervision, finite spatial memory, exposure-bias drift, and non-real-time inference are all candidly acknowledged with concrete future-work directions, plus detailed implementation/appendix material supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central assumption that ground-truth 3D voxel supervision (W, C) is available during training substantially restricts applicability to simulators/datasets with 3D annotations; while acknowledged, this weakens the generality of the 'new paradigm' claim relative to purely pixel-trained world models.

Evaluation is confined to a single domain (Luanti/Craftium voxel worlds). Although procedurally generated worlds reduce overfitting, it remains unclear how the approach transfers to non-voxel, non-semantic-labeled 3D environments or real video; no cross-domain experiment is provided.

Baseline comparison fairness is imperfect: WorldMem's FVD is only reported at 200 frames (dashes at 400/600 in Table 1), and the human study used the original authors' released models trained on Minecraft data (evaluated in Minedojo), introducing a domain/setup mismatch that the authors mitigate but cannot fully eliminate.

The learned camera model's contribution is under-quantified: Camera-GT achieves nearly identical FVD, and the claim of physical inconsistencies (Figure 11) rests on qualitative evidence only; a metric capturing camera/world physical consistency would strengthen this argument.

Practical deployment remains far: ~2.7 s/frame even for PERSIST-S (Table 14), and the fast 2/4-step configuration still runs at ~1.13 FPS, so the claimed interactivity is not yet realized; components are also trained separately with heuristic noise augmentation rather than end-to-end, leaving distribution mismatch between Wθ and Pθ predictions.

Several presentation and citation issues suggest incomplete proofreading: duplicated WorldMem entries (Xiao et al., 2025a/b), malformed references (e.g., 'Hafner et al., 20 2', 'Huang et al., 20 2'), an uncited Figure 10 entry, and inconsistent model naming (PERSIST-XL vs 'default configuration').
